children.translated_text: In the phrase 'of rasa and the rest,' the sixth case is used in the sense of specification.
Among rasa, vīrya, and the rest, dravya (substance) alone is primary.

children.text: kutaḥ te rasādayo hi yasmāt tadāśrayāḥ tadeva dravyamāśrayo yeṣāṃ ta evam ||
children.translated_text: Why? For those rasa and other factors depend on that; the very thing which is their support is dravya, and they are those whose support it is.
Therefore rasa and the rest by themselves are not apprehended.
Therefore dravya is primary.
The particle tu is used for restriction.

children.text: yattadoś ca nityābhisambandhāt yadityetadanuktam apyarthāl labhyate ||
children.translated_text: Because yad and tad are invariably connected, this word yad, though not stated, is obtained from the sense.

children.text: tenāyamarthaḥ yat rasādīnāmāśrayabhūtaṃ kāryaṃ dravyaṃ harītakyādi sthāvaraṃ chāgādi vā jaṅgamaṃ tat pañcabhūtātmakam na tu yatkāraṇaṃ dravyamākāśādi ||
children.translated_text: Thus the meaning is this: the effect-substance which is the support of rasa and the rest, whether stationary, such as harītakī, or moving, such as a goat, is composed of the five elements; but not the causal substance, such as ākāśa and the rest.

children.text: tasya hi pañcabhūtātmakatve saty ākāśādīnāṃ pṛthaktvenātmalābho na syāt ||
children.translated_text: For if that too were composed of the five elements, ākāśa and the others would not attain their own existence separately.

children.text: tataścedamākāśaṃ nāma mahābhūtam idaṃ pṛthvī nāma mahābhūtamiti gadituṃ na pāryeta sarvasya pañcamahābhūtātmakatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Then one could not say, 'this is the great element called ākāśa' and 'this is the great element called earth,' since everything would be composed of the five great elements.

children.text: na ca yatkāraṇaṃ tat kadācit kāryaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor can what is a cause ever be an effect.
Therefore only effect-substance is composed of the five great elements, not causal substance such as ākāśa.

children.text: munistu khādīnyātmā manaḥ kālo diśaśca dravyasaṃgrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But the sage says: 'The collection of dravyas consists of space and the others, self, mind, time, and directions.'
Having stated that dravya is ninefold in this way, he set forth its definition.

children.text: yathā yatrāśritāḥ karmaguṇāḥ kāraṇaṃ samavāyi yat ||
children.translated_text: As follows: 'That in which actions and qualities reside, and which is an inherent cause,'
'that is dravya.'

children.text: asyārthaḥ yatra karma pariṣyandalakṣaṇaṃ saṃyogaviyogakāraṇam samavetaśca guṇaḥ yatra śabdādayo gurvādayo vā buddhirvā parādayo vā samavetāḥ yacca kāraṇaṃ samavāyi taddravyamucyate ||
children.translated_text: Its meaning is this: that in which action, defined as movement and as the cause of conjunction and disjunction, inheres; that in which quality inheres, whether sounds and the like, heaviness and the like, cognition, or priority and the like; and that which is an inherent cause, is called dravya.
'Inherent' means this:
A cause which exists without separateness is an inherent cause.
For example, the threads are the inherent cause of a cloth.

children.text: etāni karmaguṇāśrayitvasamavāyikāraṇatvāni yadyapi sarvāṇi sarvasmin dravye na vidyante tathāpi yadyatra sambhavati tatra tena tasya dravyasya dravyatvaṃ kalpyam ||
children.translated_text: Although these properties, namely being a support of actions and qualities and being an inherent cause, are not all present in every dravya, still whichever of them is possible in a given case should be used there to establish the dravya-status of that dravya.

children.text: tadyathā manasaḥ karma guṇāśrayitvena vāyvādīnāṃ tu karmaguṇāśrayitvena samavāyi kāraṇatvena ca ||
children.translated_text: For instance, mind is established by being the support of action and qualities, while air and the others are established by being supports of action and qualities and also by being inherent causes.

children.text: nanu ākāśādīni kāraṇadravyāṇīti kathamuktaṃ yāvatākāśasya dravyatvam eva nāstīti kecit ||
children.translated_text: But, someone may object, how can ākāśa and the others be called causal substances, when some say that ākāśa does not even have dravya-status?
We answer them.
Its existence is established because its blue color is apprehended directly, just as in the case of the ocean.
Likewise poets too describe its blueness.

children.text: yathā karṇāṭasya vipulapulinā hṛdyā nadyo vahanty atinirmalāḥ kamalasubhago vāyurghrāṇaṃ vilambati māṃsalaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For example: 'The lovely rivers of Karṇāṭa, with broad sandy banks, flow exceedingly clear; the wind, beautiful with lotuses, thickly lingers at the nose.'
'The moon, as if just emerged from a dwelling shaded by a fresh raincloud, bears whiteness in the blue, glossy sky.'
So the verse says.
And similarly there is <s>Bāṇa</s>'s expression, 'in the sky washed by lightning.'
They refute this argument.

children.text: tathā hi dūrāt bhrāntimātreṇaiva nīlarūpatvam asyopalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: For, in fact, its blue color is perceived merely through an illusion caused by distance.
Just as a mountain, though of various colors, appears blue from afar.
The poets' description is to be regarded as lacking proof, based only on a slight resemblance.
Similarly they describe fire as white.
But whiteness is not possible for it, because it is without definite shape.
Therefore blue color is not possible for ākāśa.

children.text: api ca yadyākāśasya nīlarūpatā syāt tadā nīlarūpaṃ bhaven nabhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, if ākāśa had blue color, then the sky would be blue in color.
But a glossy blue color could not belong to the sky.
Objection: because perception varies, it is reasonable that it should possess color.

children.text: yathā puruṣaḥ śarāder ṛjutāṃ didṛkṣurekaṃ cakṣurnimīlyāparaṃ conmīlya tāmupalabhate na tu nayanayugalena ||
children.translated_text: For example, a man wishing to see the straightness of an arrow and the like perceives it by closing one eye and opening the other, but not with both eyes together.

children.text: tadvat saṃnikṛṣṭe gaganarūpasyānādānam viprakṛṣṭe tu grahaṇaṃ syāditi ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, the color of the sky might not be grasped when it is near, but might be grasped when it is distant.
This too is not sound.

children.text: yato rūpavattve 'bhyupagamyamāne sparśavattvamasya prasajyeta rūpasya sparśena nityasambandhāt ||
children.translated_text: For if it is admitted to possess color, it would follow that it also possesses touch, because color is invariably connected with touch.
And if it possessed touch, it would not have the very nature of ākāśa.
Therefore vyoman, space, does not possess color.
Others, however, think as follows.
Let ākāśa have a condition like wind.

children.text: yathā kila pavanaḥ sparśavān na ca tasmin rūpaṃ sambhavati ||
children.translated_text: For wind, they say, has touch, yet color is not possible in it.
In just the same way ākāśa may possess color and yet not possess touch.
This is the prattle of people who have not understood the nature of categories.

children.text: tato yatra rūpaṃ tatrāvaśyaṃ sparśaḥ na tu yatra sparśas tatrāvaśyaṃ rūpam ||
children.translated_text: For wherever there is color, there is necessarily touch; but wherever there is touch, there is not necessarily color.

children.text: tasmān na nabho rūpavanna ca sat ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the sky neither possesses color nor is it nonexistent.
On this point the reply is given:
That on the basis of which origination is taught by those who see reality exists.
For example, earth and the other elements.

children.text: uktaṃ ca akṣarāt khaṃ tato vāyustasmāttejas tato jalam ||
children.translated_text: And it has been said: 'From the imperishable came space; from that, wind; from that, fire; from that, water.'
'From water earth was born: this is the arising of the elements.'
So the verse says.
Therefore ākāśa exists as a dravya.
Moreover, because particular phenomena such as movement, growth, and birth are apprehended with ākāśa as their basis, ākāśa exists.
Just as the eye is inferred from the possibility of the particular apprehension of color.

children.text: api ca ākāśābhāve hy ekaghanatvaṃ jagataḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, if there were no ākāśa, the world would be a single compact mass.
Likewise, because otherwise the quality called sound could not be accounted for, there is <s>ākāśa</s>.
But, one might object, air has no substantiality, because there is no means of knowledge that grasps its own nature.

children.text: sparśopalabdher vāyor astitvamucyata iti cet tadapi na yato 'dhunaivoktaṃ khādvāyuriti ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that the existence of air is asserted from the perception of touch, that too is not so, because it has just now been stated that air arises from ether.

children.text: gaganasya ca sparśābhāvād vāyor apy asparśavattvaṃ kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvāt kāryasya ||
children.translated_text: And since the sky is without touch, air too would have the property of being without touch, because an effect is preceded by the qualities of its cause.
This is not so.
For an effect is observed to be of both kinds.

children.text: kāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ kāryaṃ dṛṣṭam akāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ ca dṛṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: An effect is seen to be preceded by the qualities of its cause, and it is also seen not to be preceded by the qualities of its cause.

children.text: tatra kāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ tāvadyathā tantuśvetatvapūrvakaṃ paṭe śvetatvaṃ dṛṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: Among these, what is preceded by the quality of its cause is, for instance, the whiteness seen in a cloth, preceded by the whiteness of its threads.

children.text: akāraṇaguṇapūrvakaṃ ca dṛṣṭam yathā haridrākṣārasaṃyogād raktatā ||
children.translated_text: And what is not preceded by the quality of its cause is seen, for instance, in redness arising from the conjunction of turmeric and alkali.
Therefore air, though produced from touchless <s>ākāśa</s>, can indeed possess touch.

children.text: nanu evam apyagnijalapṛthivīṣvapi sparśaviśeṣasambhavāt agnyādisamavāya eva vāyur vyavahriyate na tu tadvyatirikto vāyur asti ||
children.translated_text: But, even so, because a special touch is possible also in fire, water, and earth, what is called air is only inherence in fire and the rest; there is no air distinct from them.
To this it is said:

children.text: satyamanalādīnām api sparśo'sti kiṃtu vilakṣaṇa evāsau ||
children.translated_text: True, fire and the others also have touch, but that touch is indeed of a different kind.
For thus the touch of fire inheres in the same object as color alone.
The touch of water is co-inherent with color and taste.
The touch of earth is co-inherent with color, taste, and smell.
But the touch that belongs to air inheres in actions such as the movement of leaves and the breaking of branches.

children.text: sa naiṣāmagnyādīnāṃ dṛṣṭānāṃ nāpy adṛṣṭānām ātmadikkālādīnām ||
children.translated_text: That is not found in these visible things such as fire, nor in invisible things such as self, direction, time, and so on.

children.text: guṇāś ca sarve dravyāśrayā dṛṣṭāḥ rūpādaya iva paṭādiṣu ||
children.translated_text: And all qualities are observed to have substances as their supports, just as color and the like have cloth and similar things as their supports.
Therefore, from air’s possession of a distinctive touch, its existence is inferred.
Likewise, the existence of wind is established from the teaching of its action.
That whose action is taught by those who see reality exists.

children.text: yathā kaphādivadvātasya ca karmopadiṣṭam sraṃsavyāsavyadhasvāpa ityādi ||
children.translated_text: For example, as in the case of phlegm and the like, the action of <s>vāta</s> has been taught: slipping, expanding, piercing, causing sleep, and so forth.
Therefore air exists as a <s>dravya</s> (substance).
Fire is not a substance, one may object, because it is not perceived apart from fuel.
To this it is said:
The existence of fire is established because those who see reality teach it as a cause for the production of substances.
And accordingly, in this very text it will say: 'What is fiery consists of burning, manifestation, color, illumination, and cooking.'
Thus.

children.text: nanu yuktaś caturṇāṃ pṛthivyāptejovāyūnāṃ bhūtānāṃ sāvayavatvāt dravyeṣūtkarṣāpakarṣasaṃniveśaḥ kvaciddravye kasyacidbhūtasya pramāṇataḥ prabhāvataś cāvayavānām utkarṣāpakarṣasadbhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object, in the case of the four elements earth, water, fire, and air, because they have parts, the arrangement of increase and decrease among substances is reasonable, since in a given substance there is, by measure and by potency, an increase or decrease of the parts of some element.

children.text: ākāśasya tu niravayavatvāt sūkṣmatvād ekatvāc cotkarṣāpakarṣasaṃniveśo na yuktaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But in the case of <s>ākāśa</s>, because it is without parts, subtle, and single, an arrangement of increase and decrease is not reasonable.
What you say is reasonable.

children.text: kiṃtu sāvayavānāmeva dravyāṇāṃ ye 'vayavāḥ kvacitpāṣāṇādau saṃhatās tathāvatiṣṭhante ||
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, the parts of substances that do have parts sometimes remain compacted together, as in stone and the like.

children.text: yathā tatra dravye kāṭhinyasya prakarṣo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: For example, in that substance there is a predominance of hardness.
There <s>ākāśa</s> is diminished.
But when the arrangement of parts is not dense, <s>ākāśa</s> is predominant.
Thus, by this reasoning, a lesser and greater state is possible even for <s>ākāśa</s>.
It arises with earth made its support.

children.text: evaṃ pṛthvyākhyena bhūtenādhāratvenopakṛtya tena tadārabdhaṃ dravyam ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, when the element called earth assists as a support, a substance begun by that is so called.

children.text: tathā ambu salilaṃ yoniḥ kāraṇaṃ yasya tadambuyoni dravyam ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, a substance whose womb, that is, cause, is water or liquid is called water-born.

children.text: evaṃ jalaṃ nāma mahābhūtaṃ rasavattvād yonitayopakṛtya tena tadārabdham ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus the great element called water, because it possesses taste, assists as womb or source, and a substance begun by that is so called.
The sage too has said: 'Taste is for the purpose of the tongue; its substance is water, and also earth.'

children.text: nirvṛttau ca viśeṣe ca pratyayāḥ khādayastrayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'And in production and in differentiation, the three factors beginning with ether are the conditions.'
Thus.
With regard to these substances and so on, the distinction between support and action is to be considered.

children.text: tathā agnipavananabhasāṃ samavāyāt apṛthagbhāvāt tasya dravyasya nirvṛttiḥ niṣpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the inherence and non-separateness of fire, wind, and ether comes the production, the accomplishment, of that substance.

children.text: tathā tasya dravyasya yo viśeṣaḥ idamanyadidamanyad dravyam ityevaṃrūpo nānāsvabhāvaḥ so 'pyagnipavananabhasāṃ samavāyāt ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, the specific character of that substance, the manifold nature expressed as 'this substance is one thing, this is another,' also comes from the inherence of fire, wind, and ether.

children.text: evam agnipavananabhobhiḥ samavāyikāraṇatvenopakṛtya tair etad dravyamārabdham ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, when fire, wind, and ether assist as inherent causes, this substance is said to be begun by them.

children.text: eva ca sarvaṃ kāryadravyaṃ pañcamahābhūtātmakam pañcabhir mahābhūtair ārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: In this way every produced substance consists of the five great elements, because it is begun by the five great elements.

children.text: yatra dravye yad bhūtaṃ bhūyiṣṭham adhikṛtaṃ tena tasya vyapadeśaḥ saṃjñā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Whichever element is most abundant or predominant in a substance, by that its designation, its name, is made.

children.text: yathā pṛthivyādhikyotpāditaṃ dravyaṃ pārthivam evam āpyaṃ taijasaṃ ca vedyam ||
children.translated_text: For example, a substance produced by predominance of earth is earthy; similarly one should understand watery and fiery substances.

children.text: tad evaṃ sarvaṃ dravyaṃ pañcabhūtātmakaṃ sthitam ||
children.translated_text: Thus every substance is established as consisting of the five elements.

children.text: tasmād bhūtasaṃghātasambhavāt kāraṇāddravyaṃ naikarasam api tv anekarasam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because a substance arises from an aggregation of elements as its cause, it does not have a single taste, but many tastes.
As with substance, so too taste arises from an aggregation of elements.

children.text: ata eva prati dravyaṃ madhurādirasasya nānāsvādopalambhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason, in each substance a diversity of flavor is perceived in sweet and other tastes.

children.text: tathā ca drākṣākṣoḍakṣīrekṣukṣaudragokṣurādau dravye satyapi mādhurye 'paro 'para āsvāda upalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, although sweetness exists in substances such as grapes, walnuts, milk, sugarcane, honey, and <s>gokṣura</s>, a distinct flavor is perceived in each one.
In the same way, among sour substances too, such as citron and fermented grain-sour preparations, a diversity of flavors is perceived.
In the same way this is to be understood also for salty substances and the rest.

children.text: api caiṣāṃ drākṣādīnām anekarasatvam āsvādaviśeṣādanumīyamānaṃ bhūyasā rasenānyarasābhibhavaṃ kṛtvā vyapadiśyate idaṃ madhuram idam amlādyanyatamam mahābhūtavat ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, although these substances such as grapes have many tastes, this is inferred from their particular flavors; yet by the stronger taste suppressing the other tastes, they are designated, 'this is sweet,' 'this is sour,' or any one of the others, just as in the case of the great elements.

children.text: yathā sarvaṃ dravyaṃ pañcamahābhūtātmakaṃ bhūyasā mahābhūtenānyamahābhūtābhibhavaṃ kṛtvā yathā tena vyapadiśyate pārthivamidam āpyam idamiti ||
children.translated_text: For just as every substance consists of the five great elements, and is designated by that element which is more abundant, after it has suppressed the other great elements, as 'this is earthy' or 'this is watery,' so too here.

children.text: nanu dravyanirṇaye prakṛte pāñcabhautikaṃ yadeva dravyaṃ pratijñātaṃ tadeva tasmād ityādinā nigamagranthenātivāhayituṃ yuktam na punaraprastutam anekarasatvam ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object, in the present determination of substance, the very substance consisting of the five elements that has been stated should properly be carried through by the concluding text beginning 'therefore'; the irrelevant topic of manifold taste should not be introduced again.

children.text: tasmādatraivaṃ granthaḥ kartuṃ nyāyyaḥ tasmān naikabhūtajaṃ dravyaṃ bhūtasaṃghātasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the text here ought to be formulated thus: 'Therefore a substance is not born from one element, because it arises from an aggregate of elements.'
Thus.
To this it is said:
Water is the source of all six tastes.

children.text: tataścaikasyaiva mahābhūtasyodakasaṃjñasya rasakāraṇatvaṃ prāptaṃ nānyeṣām nīrasatvāt ||
children.translated_text: And from that it would follow that only one great element, called water, is the cause of taste, not the others, because they are without taste.
Therefore taste would not arise from an aggregate of elements.

children.text: ity evaṃvidhām āśaṅkām apaninīṣur bhūtasaṃghātasambhavatvaṃ rasasya caikenaiva prayatnena tasmān naikarasaṃ dravyaṃ bhūtasaṃghātasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Desiring to remove such a doubt, and to establish at one and the same effort that taste arises from an aggregate of elements, he said: 'Therefore a substance does not have only one taste, because it arises from an aggregate of elements.'
Thus he spoke.

children.text: muniścāta eva rasasya bhūtasaṃghātasambhavatvaṃ spaṣṭaṃ kṛtvovāca ||
children.translated_text: And for this very reason the sage, making clear that taste arises from an aggregate of elements, said:
'As taste is for the purpose of tasting, its substance is water, and also earth;'

children.text: nirvṛttau ca viśeṣe ca pratyayāḥ khādayas trayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'and in its production and in its differentiation, the three beginning with ether are the conditions.'
Thus.
In this way, an aggregate of elements is the causal source of tastes, even though those tastes are supported by substances.
And this we shall explain in detail in the section on the distinctions of taste.
Since every substance has many tastes,

children.text: tataḥ tasmātkāraṇāt ekadoṣā rogā jvarādayo na bhavanti api tv anekadoṣāḥ tridoṣā ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: therefore, for that reason, diseases such as fever are not single-<s>doṣa</s> diseases, but rather have many <s>doṣa</s>s; that is, they involve the three <s>doṣa</s>s.
Here too, the phrase 'by predominance' is to be supplied in the designation.

children.text: tena tridoṣātmake'pi jvare vātādhike vātajvara evaṃ pittajvaraḥ śleṣmajvara ityevaṃrūpo vyapadeśa upapannaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, even though fever has the nature of all three <s>doṣa</s>s, when <s>vāta</s> is predominant the designation 'vāta-fever' is appropriate, and likewise 'pitta-fever' and 'śleṣman-fever.'

children.text: nanu yadi sarvo jvaraḥ saṃnipātajaḥ tatkimiti vakṣyati ayaṃ saṃnipātajvara iti ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object, if every fever is produced by the conjunction of the <s>doṣa</s>s, why will the author say, 'this is a saṃnipāta-fever'?
We reply:

children.text: samaviṣamarūpaṃ śaktyutkarṣamāśritya yatra doṣā vartante sa saṃnipātajvara iti tantrakṛtā purastādvistareṇa pratipādayiṣyate ||
children.translated_text: Where the <s>doṣa</s>s occur with an equal or unequal form of predominance of power, that is called saṃnipāta-fever; this will be explained at length by the author of the treatise later on.
Now, asking what is <s>rasa</s> and what is <s>anurasa</s>, he says 'there,' and so on.

children.text: tatra tasmin dravye yo vyaktaḥ sphuṭa upalabhyate sa rasaḥ smṛtas tantrakṛdbhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, in that substance, what is clearly and distinctly perceived is remembered by the authors of the treatise as <s>rasa</s>.
And what is indistinct, appearing unclearly, but is perceived by the organ of taste, is <s>anurasa</s>.
Here the prefix 'anu' has a sense of deficiency; it means a slight taste.
And this alone is not the definition of <s>anurasa</s>, so he says 'somewhat,' and so on.

children.text: mukhakṣiptasya harītakyāder dravyasya rasanendriyeṇa kiṃcid ante vyakto 'pyupalabhyate yaḥ so 'pyanurasa iṣyate munibhiriti vākyaśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When a substance such as harītakī has been put into the mouth, the taste which is somewhat perceived by the organ of taste even clearly at the end is also accepted by the sages as <s>anurasa</s>; this is the remainder of the sentence.

children.text: ante ityanenaitad bodhayati ante avasāne na tv ādāv āpātamātre na ca madhye ||
children.translated_text: By the word 'at the end' he indicates this: at the end, in the final phase, not at the beginning, at the mere first contact, nor in the middle.
For at those two times there is perception only of the main <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: anuśabdasyātra paścādarthatvāt paścāt sphuṭo'pi kiṃcid ya upalabhyate so 'pyanurasa ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since the word 'anu' here has the sense of 'afterward,' the meaning is that what is perceived afterward, even somewhat distinctly, is also <s>anurasa</s>.

children.text: pṛthivyādau pṛthivyādimahābhūtārabdhe dravye rasāśraye gurvādayo guṇāḥ paramārthata āśritāḥ na tu raseṣu madhurādiṣu ||
children.translated_text: In substances beginning with earth, that is, in substances produced from the great elements beginning with earth and serving as supports of taste, qualities such as heaviness truly reside, but not in the tastes such as sweet.
But when they are designated in tastes, that is by figurative usage based on concomitance.

children.text: saha caratīti sahacaraḥ tasya bhāvaḥ sāhacaryam ||
children.translated_text: That which accompanies is a concomitant; the state of that is concomitance.

children.text: yasminneva guḍādau dravye madhuro rasa āśritastasminnapi guruguṇa āśritaḥ iti madhurarasaguruguṇayoḥ sahacarabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the very same substance such as jaggery in which the sweet taste is based, the quality of heaviness is also based; thus there is a relation of concomitance between sweet taste and the quality of heaviness.

children.text: sāhacaryeṇa tulyāśrayatvenopacāraḥ sāhacaryopacāraḥ tasmāt sāhacaryopacārato gurvādayo guṇā raseṣu madhurādiṣu vyapadiśyante ||
children.translated_text: A figurative usage based on concomitance, because of having the same substratum, is sāhacaryopacāra; therefore, by figurative usage based on concomitance, qualities such as heaviness are designated in tastes such as sweet.
For example, people say 'the sweet taste is heavy' and 'the sour taste is light,' and so on.

children.text: na punaḥ paramārthato raseṣu gurvādayaḥ santi ||
children.translated_text: But qualities such as heaviness do not truly exist in the tastes themselves.
And designation by concomitance is indeed found.

children.text: yathā ghṛtasahacareṇa ghṛtasthenāgninā dagdho ghṛtadagdha ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: For example, one burned by fire that accompanies ghee, that is, fire present in ghee, is said to be 'burned by ghee.'

children.text: tatra teṣu pārthivādiṣu pañcasu dravyeṣu madhye pārthivaṃ dravyaṃ gurvādiguṇotkaṭam ||
children.translated_text: There, among those five substances such as the earthy and the rest, an earthy substance is predominant in qualities such as heaviness.

children.text: ulbaṇaśabdenaitat dyotayati pārthive dravye 'nye'pi guṇāḥ santi sarvadravyāṇāṃ pāñcabhautikatvāt gurvādayastatrotkaṭāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The word 'predominant' indicates this: in an earthy substance there are other qualities too, because all substances consist of the five elements, but qualities such as heaviness are predominant there.
In the same way everything should be applied to watery substances and the rest.
Thus 'bringing about heaviness and the like' means producing heaviness and the like.
A watery substance is predominant in qualities such as fluidity and produces moistening and the like.
A fiery substance is predominant in qualities such as dryness and causes burning and the like.
An airy substance is predominant in qualities such as dryness and produces roughness, lightness, and the like.
An ethereal substance is predominant in qualities such as subtlety and produces hollowness and the like.

children.text: evam anena pañcamahābhūtārabdhena gurvādiguṇayogena dravyāṇāṃ jagati bhuvane'smin anauṣadhabhūtaṃ na kiṃcid dravyamasti api tu sarvam eva dravyaṃ yatsikatāpāṃsvādikaṃ tadauṣadhaṃ cikitsitam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, by this account, since substances are begun from the five great elements and are joined with qualities such as heaviness, there is no substance in this world, this inhabited realm, that is not medicinal. Rather, every substance, even sand, dust, and the like, is medicine, that is, something used in treatment.

children.text: vaśānnānārthayogayoḥ arthaśca yogaśca arthayogau arthaḥ prayojanam yogo yuktiḥ yathā anayā yuktyauṣadhamidaṃ yojitamasya rogasya vijayāya syādanayā cāsya rogasyeti nānāvidhau yāv arthayogau tayorvaśātsāmarthyāt sarvamapi dravyamauṣadham rogapratīkārahetutvāt ||
children.translated_text: Because of the conjunction of various purposes and methods: purpose and method are the two, purpose-and-method. Purpose means the intended aim; method means the practical reasoning, as in: by this method this medicine is applied for the overcoming of this disease, and by this other method for that disease. By the force, that is, the capacity, of these various purposes and methods, every substance is medicine, since it is a cause for counteracting disease.
It is called upward-moving because it goes upward.
In the grammatical section on kha, the root gam is also additionally enumerated; therefore the suffix kha is used.

children.text: prāyo bāhulyena ūrdhvagamaṃ dravyam agnipavanādhikaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Generally, for the most part, an upward-moving substance is one in which fire and wind predominate.
For example, madana fruit and the like.
Because the word 'mostly' is included, downward movement is also observed even in something strongly marked by fire and wind.
For example, in harītakī and the like, because their specific potency is inconceivable.
Just as the jewel on a serpent's hood, though the serpent is full of poison, is an antidote to poison.
For the most part, a substance in which earth and water are predominant moves downward.
For example, trivṛt and the like.

children.text: yattu vyāmiśrātmakaṃ tulyakālam ūrdhvādhodoṣaharaṇaṃ tadiha granthagauravabhayān noktamapi vyāmiśrabhūtotkaṭaṃ dravyaṃ vyāmiśrātmakamiti sāmarthyalabdha evāyamarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But a substance of mixed nature that removes the doṣas upward and downward at the same time has not been mentioned here from fear of prolixity. Still, the meaning is obtained by implication: a substance in which mixed elements predominate is of mixed nature.

children.text: iti parisamāptau dravyaṃ prati yad vaktavyaṃ tan niṣpannam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The word iti marks completion: what had to be said concerning substance has been completed; that is the meaning.

children.text: bahuvaktavyatvād uttaratra anantare 'dhyāye rasān bhedaiḥ triṣaṣṭisaṃkhyāvacchinnaiḥ upadekṣyate tantrakṛt ||
children.translated_text: Because there is much to say, in the next, immediately following chapter, the author of the treatise will teach the tastes by their distinctions, limited to the number sixty-three.
Substance has been explained.

children.text: vīryaṃ punargurvādīn aṣṭau guṇān dravyāśritān iti samācakṣate ||
children.translated_text: As for vīrya, they define it as the eight qualities beginning with heaviness, which are resident in substance.

children.text: tat tasmāt evam anena prakāreṇa vīryamaṣṭadhā aṣṭaprakāraṃ gurvādivādināṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, in this way, the doctrine of those who speak of heaviness and the rest is that vīrya is eightfold, of eight kinds.

children.text: yena svabhāvena yā kriyā kriyate yatkarma niṣpādyate tadvīryam ||
children.translated_text: The nature by which an action is performed, by which an effect is accomplished, is vīrya.

children.text: tadevaṃ yāvat kiṃcid guṇajātaṃ dravye sthitaṃ tatsarvaṃ vīryam eva ||
children.translated_text: Accordingly, whatever class of qualities is situated in a substance is all vīrya.

children.text: sarvaṃ vīryaṃ karotītyata evāha nāvīryam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Every vīrya performs an action; for just this reason he says, 'Nothing without vīrya,' and so on.

children.text: yanna vīryaṃ tanna kiṃcit karoti na kāṃcid apyarthakriyāṃ niṣpādayati pratiniyataśaktipariṣvaktatvāt sarvabhāvānām ||
children.translated_text: What is not vīrya does nothing; it does not accomplish any purposeful action, because all entities are embraced by determinate powers.
For this very reason he says, 'all,' and so on.
The word hi has the sense of 'because.'
Because every action is produced by vīrya, generated by vīrya.

children.text: tato yanna vīryaṃ tanna kiṃcit kurute ||
children.translated_text: Therefore what is not vīrya does nothing.

children.text: yato vīryasyaiva karaṇasāmarthyaṃ tena kāraṇena gurvādiṣv evāṣṭāsu vīryākhyā anvartheti anugatārtheti bhaṇyate ||
children.translated_text: Since only vīrya has the capacity to act, for that reason the name vīrya is said to apply meaningfully, that is, with its sense following, only to the eight qualities beginning with heaviness.
The word eva is for restriction.

children.text: gurvādiṣveva vīryasaṃjñā na tu rasavipākaprabhāveṣu mandasāndrādiṣu vā ||
children.translated_text: The designation vīrya belongs only to heaviness and the rest, not to taste, post-digestive effect, specific potency, or to dullness, density, and the other qualities.
What kind of heaviness and the rest? He says, 'complete,' and so on.

children.text: samagrāś ca te guṇāśca teṣu sārāḥ cirakālāvasthitayo gurvādaya eva ||
children.translated_text: Those qualities are complete, and among them the essences, that is, those that remain for a long time, are precisely heaviness and the rest.

children.text: tathā ca jāṭharāgnisaṃyogenāpi na madhurādirasavat svabhāvamete jahati ||
children.translated_text: Thus, even through conjunction with the gastric fire, these do not abandon their nature as sweet and the other tastes do.
The word sāra is formed with the suffix ghañ from the root sṛ in the sense 'firmly stable.'

children.text: tathā anyebhyo mandasāndrādibhyo guṇebhyo rasādibhyo vā gurvādayaḥ śaktyutkarṣavivartinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, compared with other qualities such as dullness and density, or compared with taste and the like, heaviness and the rest are transformations of superior power.

children.text: śakteḥ sāmarthyasya utkarṣaḥ ādhikyam viśeṣeṇa varto vivartaḥ viśeṣeṇa bhavanaṃ śaktyutkarṣasya vivartaḥ sa vidyate yeṣāṃ ta evam ||
children.translated_text: The superiority of power means an excess of capacity; vivarta means a special mode of becoming. Those in which there is such a transformation of superior power are so called.

children.text: kiṃca gurvādīnāṃ guṇānāṃ vyavahārāya vyavahārārtham mukhyatvāt anyebhyo guṇebhyo gurvādayaḥ pradhānabhūtā ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, for the sake of usage, that is, practical designation, because they are primary, the qualities beginning with heaviness are predominant over the other qualities; this is the meaning.

children.text: tathā ca gurvādayo guṇā dravye pṛthivyādau rasāśraye ||
children.translated_text: And accordingly, the qualities beginning with heaviness exist in substance, in earth and the rest, which are the supports of taste.
This has been stated, not that the qualities beginning with sweetness are qualities in that sense.
Therefore the practical primacy of the qualities beginning with heaviness is greater than that of taste and the others.

children.text: tathā bahvagragrahaṇāt bahugrahaṇād agragrahaṇāc ca bahavo dravyarasādayo gurvādibhirgṛhītā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, because of the words 'many' and 'first,' from the mention of 'many' and the mention of 'first,' many things, substances, tastes, and the like, are included under heaviness and the rest.

children.text: tathā cāyurvedaśāstreṣu rasādibhyo gurvādīnām agre grahaṇaṃ dṛṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: And in the Ayurvedic treatises, the mention of heaviness and the rest is seen to come before taste and the others.

children.text: yathā vātādidoṣaguṇanirūpaṇāyāṃ gurvādīnāmeva pūrvagrahaṇam na rasādīnām ||
children.translated_text: For example, in determining the qualities of the doṣas beginning with vāta, it is heaviness and the other qualities that are mentioned first, not taste and the others.

children.text: tathā ca tatra rūkṣo laghuḥ ityācāryo'paṭhad vāyvādilakṣaṇe ||
children.translated_text: Accordingly, there the teacher recited 'dry, light' in the characterization of vāta and the rest.

children.text: evaṃ gurvādīnām evāgragrahaṇāt gurvādiṣveva vīryākhyā 'nvarthā anugatārtheti bhaṇyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, because the qualities beginning with heaviness alone are mentioned first, the name vīrya is said to apply meaningfully, with its sense following, only to heaviness and the rest.

children.text: ato 'smācca kāraṇakadambakāt viparītatvāt vaiparītyena sthitatvāt na rasādayo vīryam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of this collection of reasons, taste and the others are not vīrya, since they stand in the opposite condition.

children.text: tathā hi rasasya sāratvaṃ nāsti jāṭharānalasaṃyogavaśena rasāntarotpatteḥ ||
children.translated_text: For taste has no essential stability, because through conjunction with the gastric fire another taste is produced.
But the qualities beginning with heaviness do not become otherwise even through conjunction with the gastric fire.

children.text: tathā ca na rasasya śaktyutkarṣavivartitvam yato rasasya gurvādyāhitaśaktereva svakarmaṇi sāmarthyam ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, taste is not a transformation of superior power, since taste has capacity for its own action only through the power imparted by heaviness and the other qualities.

children.text: vyavahārāya yathā gurvāder mukhyatvaṃ yathā ca bahvagragrahaṇaṃ tathā prāg darśitam ||
children.translated_text: As regards practical usage, the primacy of heavy and the rest, and also the inclusion of many foremost factors, has already been shown before.

children.text: prabhāvaḥ sarvātiśāyī dravyasvabhāvaḥ tasya ca kriyānirvartanasāmānye satyapi vīryasaṃjñā pūrvoktāddhetor na pravartate ||
children.translated_text: <s>Prabhāva</s> (specific efficacy) is the nature of a substance that surpasses all; and although it has the common property of accomplishing action, the designation <s>vīrya</s> (potency) does not apply to it, for the reason stated earlier.
The same should be considered also with regard to <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation) and action.

children.text: tasmāt rasādyeṣu sambhavatyapi vidyamānāpi asadrūpeva sā vīryasaṃjñā na vivakṣyate norarīkriyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, even though that designation <s>vīrya</s> is possible and present among taste and the other factors, it is as if non-existent there; it is neither intended nor accepted.
What exists at the beginning is <s>ādya</s>, 'initial.'
Because it belongs to the class beginning with <s>dik</s>, the suffix <s>yat</s> is used.

children.text: rasa ādyo yeṣāṃ prabhāvādīnāṃ ta evaṃ teṣu ||
children.translated_text: Those of which taste is first, namely <s>prabhāva</s> and the rest, are so called; among them.
'<s>Vīrya</s>,' and so on.
The word <s>hi</s> has the sense of 'because.'

children.text: yata evaṃ sā vīryasaṃjñā sambhavaty api rasādiṣu vaiparītyān na vivakṣyate ato gurvādaya eva vīryam na rasādayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since, although the designation <s>vīrya</s> is possible in taste and the rest, it is not intended there because of contradiction, therefore only heavy and the rest are <s>vīrya</s>, not taste and the rest.

children.text: anya ācāryā uṣṇaṃ śītamiti dviprakāraṃ vīryam ācakṣate ||
children.translated_text: Other teachers declare <s>vīrya</s> to be of two kinds: hot and cold.
The word <s>eva</s> is for restriction.
The meaning is that <s>vīrya</s> is only twofold, not eightfold.
And the compound particle <s>api ca</s>, 'moreover,' is used in adding a reason.
The meaning is that they too speak only with reasoning.

children.text: tāmeva yuktiṃ darśayann āha nānātmakam apītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Showing that very reasoning, he says, 'although manifold in nature,' and so on.

children.text: nānāsvabhāvam api dravyaṃ sthāvarajaṅgamādyaṃ cetanācetanam agnīṣomau mahābalau utkṛṣṭaśaktī na jātu kadācid atikrāmati nollaṅghya vartate ||
children.translated_text: A substance, though manifold in nature, such as stationary and moving, sentient and insentient, never at any time transgresses the two mighty powers, fire and soma, that is, it does not exist by overstepping them.

children.text: avaśyaṃ hi dravyaṃ kiṃcid āgneyaṃ kiṃcit saumyam ataḥ kiṃcid dravyam uṣṇavīryaṃ kiṃcic chītavīryam ||
children.translated_text: For necessarily one substance is fiery and another somatic; therefore one substance has hot <s>vīrya</s> and another has cold <s>vīrya</s>.

children.text: tathā ca muniḥ na matsyān payasā sahābhyavahriyāt
children.translated_text: And accordingly the sage says: one should not eat fish together with milk.

children.text: ubhayaṃ hy etan madhuraṃ madhuravipākaṃ śītoṣṇatvāt viruddhavīryam viruddhavīryatvāc choṇitapradūṣaṇāya ||
children.translated_text: For both of these are sweet and have sweet <s>vipāka</s>, but because one is cold and the other hot their <s>vīrya</s> is incompatible; and because their <s>vīrya</s> is incompatible, they corrupt the blood.
Thus.
Here he gives an example: 'manifest and unmanifest,' and so on.

children.text: vyaktaṃ cāvyaktaṃ ca vyaktāvyaktaṃ nānātmakam api jagattrailokyaṃ kartṛ yathā vyaktaṃ cāvyaktaṃ ca nātikrāmati tathā dravyam agnīṣomāv ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Manifest and unmanifest together are 'manifest-unmanifest'; just as the manifold world, the three worlds as agent, does not transgress the manifest and the unmanifest, so a substance does not transgress fire and soma. This is the meaning.
'Manifest' means gross, that is, visible.

children.text: sāṃkhyānāṃ tu mahadādi vyaktam avyaktaṃ pradhānaṃ puruṣaś ca ||
children.translated_text: But for the Sāṃkhyas, the manifest is <s>mahat</s> and the rest, while the unmanifest is <s>pradhāna</s> and also <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: tatra tayor uṣṇaśītayor madhye uṣṇam uṣṇavīryaṃ bhramādīn karoti ||
children.translated_text: There, among those two, hot and cold, the hot, that is hot <s>vīrya</s>, causes giddiness and the like.
<s>Āśupākitā</s> means quickness of digestion.

children.text: śiśiraṃ punaḥ śītavīryaṃ tu hlādanādīn karoti ||
children.translated_text: The cold, again, namely cold <s>vīrya</s>, causes refreshment and the like.

children.text: jāṭhareṇaudaryeṇa agninā yogāt saṃśleṣāt yat rasānāṃ pariṇāmānte jaraṇaniṣṭhākāle rasāntaraṃ rasaviśeṣaḥ udetyutpadyate sa vipāka iti smṛto munibhiḥ kathitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When, through conjunction with the gastric abdominal fire, at the end of the transformation of tastes, at the stage when digestion is completed, another taste, a specific taste, arises, that is remembered, that is stated by the sages, as <s>vipāka</s>.

children.text: svādur madhuro guḍādiḥ paṭur lavaṇaḥ saindhavādir madhuraṃ kṛtvā pacyate rasa iti sambandhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The sweet, such as molasses, and the sharp or salty, such as rock salt, are digested after becoming sweet as taste; this is the construction.
Because 'sweetly' qualifies the action, it is neuter in gender.
The meaning is that the sweet has sweet <s>vipāka</s>, and even the salty has sweet <s>vipāka</s>.

children.text: amlo raso dadhikāñjikādiḥ amlaṃ pacyate amlavipāko bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The sour taste, such as curds and sour gruel, is digested as sour; it has sour <s>vipāka</s>.
For bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes, the <s>vipāka</s> is generally pungent.
The word 'generally' should also be connected with the preceding cases.

children.text: tena vrīhistho madhuro raso'mlaṃ pacyata ityupapannam ||
children.translated_text: By this, it is reasonable that the sweet taste present in rice is digested as sour.
And so it has been said: 'Another rice, sweet, has sour <s>vipāka</s>.'

children.text: tathā harītakyā bhūyastvena yaḥ kaṣāyo rasaḥ sa madhuram eva pacyate ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, in <s>harītakī</s>, the taste that is predominantly astringent is digested only as sweet.

children.text: tathā kaṭuko rasaḥ śuṇṭhyārdrakapippalyādistho madhuraṃ pacyate ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, the pungent taste present in dry ginger, fresh ginger, long pepper, and the like is digested as sweet.

children.text: tathā coktam kaṣāyā madhurā pāke iti ||
children.translated_text: And so it has been said: 'Astringents are sweet in digestion.'

children.text: tathā nāgaraṃ dīpanaṃ vṛṣyaṃ grāhi hṛdyaṃ vibandhanut ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, '<s>nāgara</s> is kindling, aphrodisiac, absorbent, pleasant to the heart, and remover of constipation.'

children.text: rucyaṃ laghu svādupākam iti tadvadārdrakam iti ||
children.translated_text: 'It is appetizing, light, and sweet in <s>vipāka</s>; fresh ginger is like that.'

children.text: tathā śleṣmalā svāduśītārdrā ityārabhya yāvat svādupākā iti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, beginning with 'it increases phlegm, is sweet, cold, and moist,' down to 'it has sweet <s>vipāka</s>.'

children.text: atra kecidāhuḥ tiktakaṣāyayoreva kaṭuvipākatayā pittakartṛtvamāpadyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Here some say: only because bitter and astringent have pungent <s>vipāka</s>, it would follow that they produce pitta.
That is not correct.
For, because these two have cold <s>vīrya</s>, they remove pitta.
For <s>vīrya</s> overcomes both taste and <s>vipāka</s>.

children.text: vakṣyati hi rasaṃ vipākas tau vīryam iti ||
children.translated_text: Indeed he will say: 'Taste and <s>vipāka</s>, those two, are overcome by <s>vīrya</s>.'

children.text: rasair jihvāvaiṣayikair madhurāmlakaṭukaiḥ vipākakālopalabhyo madhurāmlakaṭukalakṣaṇo yo raso bhavati asau tulyaphalaḥ tulyaṃ sadṛśaṃ phalaṃ yasya sa tulyaphalaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The taste characterized as sweet, sour, or pungent that is apprehended at the time of <s>vipāka</s>, in relation to tastes that are objects of the tongue, sweet, sour, and pungent, has the same result; that which has an equal or similar result is called 'having the same result.'

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati abhyavahṛtasya madhurarasasya jāṭharāgnisaṃyogavaśāt yat rasāntaraṃ phalatayā niṣpannaṃ tat rasaiḥ sadṛśaphalam ||
children.translated_text: This is what is said: when a sweet-tasting thing has been eaten, the other taste produced as a result through conjunction with the gastric fire has an effect similar to that of the tastes.

children.text: phalagrahaṇe naitatpratipādayati phalopamam eva vṛṣyādilakṣaṇaṃ kāryasadṛśam na tu kusumopamaṃ dehāhlādanādilakṣaṇaṃ kāryam iti ||
children.translated_text: By mentioning result, he does not state merely something comparable to a result, such as the action characterized by aphrodisiac effect and the like, nor an action comparable to a flower, such as delighting the body and the like.
The same should be explained also for sour and the other tastes.
'There,' and so on.

children.text: tatra teṣu rasavīryavipākādiṣu madhye dravyaṃ kiṃcic chubhāśubhaṃ sadasatkarma rasena kurute ||
children.translated_text: There, among taste, <s>vīrya</s>, <s>vipāka</s>, and the rest, some substance performs auspicious or inauspicious, good or bad, action by means of taste.
For example, honey, by having sweet and astringent taste, pacifies pitta.
Some substance acts by means of <s>vipāka</s>.

children.text: yathā tadeva madhu kaṭuvipākatayā kaphaṃ hanti ||
children.translated_text: For example, that same honey, because it has pungent <s>vipāka</s>, destroys kapha.

children.text: kiṃcana dravyaṃ guṇāntareṇa anyonyaguṇavikṛtatvāt rasavipākato yaḥ sa guṇāntaro gurvādiḥ tena ||
children.translated_text: A certain substance acts through another quality, because it is modified by mutually interacting qualities; from the standpoint of taste and post-digestive effect, that other quality is heaviness and the like.
For example, sour <s>kāñjika</s> pacifies <s>kapha</s> because of its dryness.
A certain substance acts through potency.

children.text: yathā kaṣāyatiktaṃ mahatpañcamūlaṃ vātaṃ jayati na tu pittam uṣṇavīryatvāt ||
children.translated_text: For example, the astringent and bitter <s>mahatpañcamūla</s> conquers <s>vāta</s>, but not <s>pitta</s>, because it has hot potency.

children.text: kiṃcana dravyaṃ prabhāveṇaiva śubhāśubhaṃ karma kurute ||
children.translated_text: A certain substance performs an auspicious or inauspicious action solely through its specific efficacy.
For example, sour and hot liquor increases milk.

children.text: rasādīnāṃ rasavīryavipākaprabhāvānāṃ madhye yad rasādivastu raso vā vīryaṃ vā vipāko vā prabhāvo vā balavattvena baliṣṭhatayā dravye vartate 'vatiṣṭhate tad vastujātam itarān abaliṣṭhān abhibhūya viphalīkṛtya kāraṇatvaṃ prapadyate karmakaraṇe kāraṇatām āsādayatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among taste and the others, namely taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and specific efficacy, whichever entity among taste and the rest, whether taste, potency, post-digestive effect, or specific efficacy, exists in a substance as powerful, that is, as strongest, that class of entity overcomes the others that are not strong, renders them fruitless, and assumes causal status; the meaning is that it attains causality in the performance of an action.
Therefore he states this with the words beginning 'when opposed,' and so on.

children.text: hi yasmāt viruddhaguṇasaṃyoge saṃhatībhāve sati yadalpaṃ vastu tat bhūyasā balavatā jīyate 'bhibhūyate ||
children.translated_text: For, when there is a conjunction, an aggregated state, of opposed qualities, the small entity is conquered, that is, overcome, by the greater and stronger one.

children.text: guṇaśabdena cātra rasādayo gṛhyante na pāribhāṣikā gurvādayo 'prakṛtatvāt ||
children.translated_text: And here the word 'quality' denotes taste and the rest, not the technical qualities such as heavy and the like, because those are not the present topic.

children.text: viruddhaguṇasaṃyoga ityatra viruddhaguṇasamavetadravyasaṃyoga iti bodhyam na viruddhaguṇasaṃyoga iti ||
children.translated_text: In the expression 'conjunction of opposed qualities,' one should understand 'the conjunction of substances in which opposed qualities inhere,' not literally a conjunction of opposed qualities.

children.text: na hi guṇānāṃ saṃyogo vaktuṃ yujyate kiṃ tarhi dravyāṇām ||
children.translated_text: For it is not proper to speak of a conjunction of qualities; rather, of substances.

children.text: tathā ca muniḥ saṃyogastu dvayor bahūnāṃ vā dravyāṇāṃ saṃhatībhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And accordingly the sage says: conjunction is the aggregated state of two or of many substances.
Thus.
Opposition is twofold: by intrinsic nature and by effect.
Opposition by intrinsic nature is, for example, that between heavy and light, and between cold and hot.
Opposition by effect is, for example, the use of a conjunction of dry and hot substances when <s>vāyu</s> is to be conquered.

children.text: atra hi yo guṇānāṃ virodhaḥ sa kāryeṇa ||
children.translated_text: For here the opposition among qualities is through the effect.

children.text: tatra yadalpaṃ vastujātaṃ tat bhūyasā vastujātenābhibhūyate ||
children.translated_text: In that case, whatever class of entity is small is overcome by the greater class of entity.

children.text: tatra yathā kṣīraṃ śītavīryamapi madhurarasahetuke gauravādibhiḥ sahāyabāhulyād vātaśamanākhyaṃ kāryaṃ karoti na punaḥ svakāryaṃ vātaprakopākhyam ||
children.translated_text: For example, milk, though cold in potency, because of the abundance of assisting factors such as heaviness caused by its sweet taste, performs the action called pacification of <s>vāta</s>, and not its own action, namely the aggravation of <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: rasaṃ madhurādiṣaḍvidham vipākaḥ kartā apohati kāryakaraṇe kuṇṭhayati ||
children.translated_text: Post-digestive effect, as agent, removes taste, the sixfold group beginning with sweet; it blunts it in producing an action.

children.text: yathā madhuro madhuni rasaḥ kaṭunā vipākenābhibhūyate ata eva pavanaśamanākhyaṃ kāryaṃ madhurarasahetukaṃ na karoti api tu vātaprakopanākhyaṃ kaṭuvipākahetukameva karoti ||
children.translated_text: For example, the sweet taste in honey is overcome by the pungent post-digestive effect; for this very reason it does not perform the action called pacification of wind, which would be caused by the sweet taste, but rather performs only the action called aggravation of <s>vāta</s>, caused by the pungent post-digestive effect.
Potency, serving as the agent, removes those two, taste and post-digestive effect.

children.text: yathā mahiṣāmiṣe sthitau madhurarasavipākāv uṣṇavīryākhyaṃ kartṛ abhibhavati ata eva tanmāṃsaṃ pittādidūṣaṇam anyathā svādurasavipākitvāt pittaśamanakam eva syāt ||
children.translated_text: For example, in buffalo meat the sweet taste and post-digestive effect are overcome by the agent called hot potency; for this very reason that meat vitiates <s>pitta</s> and the others. Otherwise, because it has sweet taste and post-digestive effect, it would indeed pacify <s>pitta</s>.
But specific efficacy conquers all three, taste and the rest.
For example, liquor, though sour in taste and post-digestive effect and hot in potency, produces milk.

children.text: balasāmye itīdṛśam rasādīnāṃ naisargikaṃ balaṃ svābhāvikī śaktiḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'When strength is equal': such is the natural strength of taste and the others, their innate power.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati rasaṃ samabalamapi vipāko'pohati rasavipākau ca samabalāv api vīryaṃ svabhāvādapohati etāni ca samabalānyapi prabhāvo 'pohatīti ||
children.translated_text: This is what is meant: post-digestive effect removes taste even when it is of equal strength; potency, by its nature, removes taste and post-digestive effect even when they are of equal strength; and specific efficacy removes these even when they are of equal strength.

children.text: dvayor dravyayor rasādīnāṃ rasavīryavipākānāṃ sāmye sati yadekaṃ dravyamanyatkarma kurute anyatpunaranyadviśiṣṭaṃ karma tat prabhāvajaṃ prabhāvāj jātam iti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: When, in two substances, taste and the others, namely taste, potency, and post-digestive effect, are the same, if one substance performs one action while the other performs a different, distinctive action, that should be understood as born from specific efficacy, produced from <s>prabhāva</s>.

children.text: ayamasya dravyasya prabhāva iti viśiṣṭakarmakaraṇānniścīyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that 'this is the specific efficacy of this substance' is determined from its performance of a distinctive action.

children.text: nanu prabhāvaḥ ka ucyate iti cet brūmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If one asks, 'What is called specific efficacy?' we reply:

children.text: rasavīryavipākādiguṇātiśāyī dravyasya svabhāvo yaḥ sa prabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That nature of a substance which surpasses the qualities such as taste, potency, and post-digestive effect is specific efficacy.
And it has been said:
That which fully possesses an excellence beyond the qualities beginning with taste, potency, and post-digestive effect,

children.text: dravyasvabhāvo nirdiṣṭo yaḥ prabhāvaḥ sa kīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the nature of a substance so described, that is called specific efficacy.
Thus.

children.text: citrakasya rasavīryavipākaistulyāpi dantī rasādibhyo 'tiśāyidravyasvabhāvayogād virecanī na citrakaḥ citrakatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Although <s>dantī</s> is equal to <s>citraka</s> in taste, potency, and post-digestive effect, <s>dantī</s> is purgative because it possesses a substance-nature surpassing taste and the rest, while <s>citraka</s> is not, because it is <s>citraka</s>.

children.text: madhukasya ca mṛdvīkā tulyāpi rasādibhyo 'tiśāyidravyasvabhāvayogāt mṛdvīkā virecanī na madhukam ||
children.translated_text: And although grapes are equal to <s>madhuka</s>, because they possess a substance-nature surpassing taste and the rest, grapes are purgative, while <s>madhuka</s> is not.

children.text: ghṛtaṃ kṣīrasya rasādibhistulyamapi ghṛtaṃ dīpanam na punaḥ kṣīram ||
children.translated_text: Ghee, though equal to milk in taste and the rest, is digestive-kindling, while milk is not.

children.text: anye prabhāvalakṣaṇam anyathāha prativastu svasaṃjñāpravṛttinimittalakṣaṇo yo dharmas tv atalādipratyayapratītisamadhigamyaḥ sa prabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Others state the definition of specific efficacy differently: the property in each object, characterized as the cause for the application of its own name, and understood through the suffixes <s>tva</s>, <s>tā</s>, and the like, is specific efficacy.
And in another treatise it is said:

children.text: vastūnāṃ yaḥ svasaṃjñāyāḥ pravṛttau kāraṇe smṛtaḥ
children.translated_text: That which is remembered as the cause for the application of an object's own name,

children.text: tv atalādiprabodhyaśca prabhāva iti sa smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and which is made known by <s>tva</s>, <s>tā</s>, and the like, that is remembered as specific efficacy.
Thus.

children.text: evaṃ ca dantītvād dantyā virecanakāritvaṃ prabhāvaḥ citrakasya citrakatvād avirecanakāritvaṃ prabhāvaḥ evaṃ mṛdvīkātvān mṛdvīkāyā virecanakāritvaṃ prabhāvaḥ ityādi sakalapadārtheṣu bodhyam ||
children.translated_text: Accordingly, because of <s>dantī</s>-ness, the purgative action of <s>dantī</s> is its specific efficacy; because of <s>citraka</s>-ness, the non-purgative action of <s>citraka</s> is its specific efficacy. In the same way, because of grape-ness, the purgative action of grapes is specific efficacy, and so on; this should be understood for all entities.

children.text: itiprakāre anena prakāreṇa dravyarasavīryādīnāṃ sāmānyena karma vyākhyātam na viśeṣeṇa ||
children.translated_text: In this manner, by this method, the action of substance, taste, potency, and the others has been explained in general, not in particular.

children.text: yair eva mahābhūtai rasavīryādayo dravyāśritā ārabdhāḥ tair eva tathābhūtais tadāśrayam api dravyam ||
children.translated_text: By whatever <s>mahābhūtas</s> the taste, <s>vīrya</s>, and so on, resting in a substance, have been produced, by those same elements, being of that very kind, the substance which is their support is also produced.
Therefore the action of substances and the rest has been stated in general terms.

children.text: sāmprataṃ viśiṣṭaṃ karma pratidravyaṃ vaktum idam āha punaśca taditi ||
children.translated_text: Now, in order to state the specific action for each substance, he says this: 'And again, that ...'

children.text: tatsāmānyoktaṃ karma dravyarasādīnāṃ sambandhi punarbhidyate viśiṣyate ||
children.translated_text: That action, stated generally and connected with substance, taste, and the rest, is again divided, that is, differentiated.
By what? He says, 'by varied causes,' and so on.

children.text: vicitrāśca te pratyayāśca vicitrapratyayāḥ nānākārasaṃniveśaviśeṣayuktāni mahābhūtāni pratisattvaṃ prāktanaśubhāśubhakarmaprerito vicitro mahābhūtapariṇāma ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Varied causes' means causes that are diverse: <s>mahābhūtas</s> furnished with particular arrangements of many forms; the meaning is that in each living being there is a varied transformation of the <s>mahābhūtas</s>, impelled by former good and bad karma.

children.text: vicitrapratyayārabdhaṃ ca taddravyaṃ ca tasya bhedo viśeṣaḥ tena vicitrapratyayārabdhadravyabhedena tat sāmānyoktaṃ karma dravyādīnāṃ bhidyate nānātvena sampadyate ||
children.translated_text: And that substance which is produced by varied causes has a difference, a specific character; by that difference of substance produced from varied causes, that generally stated action of substances and the rest is divided, that is, it becomes manifold.

children.text: dravyāśritatvād rasādīnāmapi yatkarma tadapi dravyabhedena bhidyate ||
children.translated_text: Since tastes and the rest rest in a substance, whatever action belongs to them is also divided according to the difference of the substance.

children.text: nanu sarvamapi deśakālādivaśād vicitrapratyayārabdham parasparavailakṣaṇyād dravyāṇām ||
children.translated_text: Objection: Is not everything produced from varied causes, under the influence of place, time, and so on, because substances are mutually distinct?
And in their mutual distinctness, the very fact of being produced from varied causes is the reason.

children.text: yadvaśādanyadidaṃ dravyamiti rūparasavīryavipākādibhinnam utpadyate tathā pratibhāsate ca ||
children.translated_text: Through its influence, one substance arises as different from another in form, taste, <s>vīrya</s>, <s>vipāka</s>, and the like, and is also perceived as such.
So what, then, is divided by the difference of a substance produced from varied causes?
Thus runs the objection.
To this we reply.

children.text: satyam etat kiṃtu viśiṣṭadravyasya saṃgrahārthaṃ vicitrapratyayārabdhamiti viśeṣaṇaṃ śāstrakṛtā kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: This is true; but the author of the treatise used the qualifier 'produced from varied causes' in order to include a particular kind of substance.

children.text: yasya bhedena dravye rasavīryādīnāṃ yatsāmānyoktaṃ karma tad bhidyate ||
children.translated_text: By the difference of that substance, the action generally stated for taste, <s>vīrya</s>, and the rest in a substance is divided.

children.text: yasmin dravye rasādīnāmanyāni mahābhūtānyārambhakāṇi dravyasya cārambhakāṇyaparāṇi tad dravyaṃ vicitrapratyayārabdham ||
children.translated_text: A substance is 'produced from varied causes' when the <s>mahābhūtas</s> that produce the tastes and the rest in that substance are one set, and those that produce the substance itself are another set.
Thus substances are of two kinds.

children.text: yataḥ kāniciddravyāṇi yair eva mahābhūtair yathāvidhai rasādaya ārabdhāḥ tair eva tathāvidhair mahābhūtais tadāśrayāṇyapi dravyāṇy ārabdhāni ||
children.translated_text: For some substances are produced, as supports, by exactly those <s>mahābhūtas</s>, and of exactly such kinds, by which the tastes and the rest have been produced.
These are called 'produced from causes identical with those of taste and the rest.'

children.text: tāni ca yathāyathaṃ tatkarma rasādyanuguṇaṃ sāmānyāt kurvate ||
children.translated_text: And, according to each case, they generally perform an action conforming to that action of taste and the rest.
For example, milk, sugarcane, sugar, and the like.

children.text: kānicit punas tadāśritarasādisamārambhakamahābhūtāny anyāni tadāśrayadravyārambhakāṇy anyāni ca mahābhūtāni tair ārabdhāni tāni vicitrapratyayārabdhāni dravyāṇi ||
children.translated_text: But in some cases the <s>mahābhūtas</s> that produce the tastes and the rest resting in a substance are one set, and the <s>mahābhūtas</s> that produce the supporting substance are another; the substances produced by those are substances produced from varied causes.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati rasādīnāmārambhakāṇy anyāni dravyasya cārambhakāṇy anyathābhūtāni mahābhūtāni nobhayatraikarūpāṇīti ||
children.translated_text: This is what is meant: the <s>mahābhūtas</s> that produce tastes and the rest are one kind, and the <s>mahābhūtas</s> that produce the substance are of another kind; they are not uniform in both cases.

children.text: tāni ca yathāyathaṃ rasādyanuguṇaṃ karma na kurvanti bhinnatvāddhetubhāvasya ||
children.translated_text: And these substances do not, according to each case, perform an action conforming to taste and the rest, because their causal condition is different.

children.text: tathā hi rasādīnām ārambhe 'nyo heturanyaśca tadāśrayadravyārambha iti ||
children.translated_text: For so it is: one cause operates in producing tastes and the rest, and another in producing the substance that is their support.
For example, <s>makuṣṭha</s>, barley, fish, lion, and the like.

children.text: etāni hi yathārasaṃ na vīryavipākakarma kurvanti vicitrapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: For these do not perform the action of <s>vīrya</s>, <s>vipāka</s>, and so on according to their taste, because they are produced from varied causes.

children.text: itthaṃ yāni rasādisamānapratyayārabdhāni dravyāṇi bahūnyapi teṣāṃ rasopadeśena karma nirdeṣṭuṃ śakyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, for substances produced from causes identical with those of taste and the rest, even though they are many, their action can be indicated by teaching their taste.

children.text: ata eva hetoḥ ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāṃ yo guṇanirdeśaḥ tasya sārthakatvam ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason, the statement of the qualities of the six tastes is meaningful.

children.text: rasopadeśamantareṇa hi bahutarāṇāṃ dravyāṇāṃ samānarūpāṇāṃ kṣīrekṣvādīnāṃ karma vaktuṃ sukhena śakyate ||
children.translated_text: For without a teaching of taste, the action of very many substances of similar form, such as milk, sugarcane, and the like, can be stated easily.

children.text: yāni tu vicitrapratyayārabdhāni dravyāṇi teṣāṃ pratidravyaṃ karmopadeśaṃ vinā yathāyathaṃ karma vaktuṃ na śakyate ||
children.translated_text: But for substances produced from varied causes, their action cannot be stated in each case without teaching the action substance by substance.

children.text: svādurasopeto guruguṇayuktaś ca godhūmo madhurarasopadiṣṭaṃ vātajittvaṃ yat karma tatkaroti samānapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Wheat, endowed with sweet taste and joined with the heavy quality, performs the action of conquering <s>vāta</s> that is taught for sweet taste, because it is produced from identical causes.

children.text: yavastu svādurasopeto guruguṇayuktaśca madhurarasopadiṣṭaṃ yadvātajittvaṃ karma tanna karoti api tu vātakṛttvameva karoti vicitrapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Barley, however, though endowed with sweet taste and joined with the heavy quality, does not perform the action of conquering <s>vāta</s> that is taught for sweet taste; rather, it actually causes <s>vāta</s>, because it is produced from varied causes.

children.text: matsyaḥ svādurasopeto guruguṇopetaśca na madhurarasopadiṣṭaḥ śītavīryaḥ kiṃ tarhi uṣṇavīryaḥ vicitrapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Fish, though endowed with sweet taste and with the heavy quality, is not cold in <s>vīrya</s> as taught for sweet taste; what then? It is hot in <s>vīrya</s>, because it is produced from varied causes.

children.text: kṣīraṃ ca svādurasopetaṃ guruguṇayuktaṃ ca madhurarasopadiṣṭaṃ śītavīryam samānapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Milk, however, is endowed with sweet taste and joined with the heavy quality, and is cold in <s>vīrya</s> as taught for sweet taste, because it is produced from identical causes.

children.text: svādurasayukto guruguṇayuktaśca siṃho na yathārasaṃ madhuravipākaḥ kiṃ tarhi kaṭuko vipāke vicitrapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: A lion, though possessed of sweet taste and the heavy quality, does not have sweet <s>vipāka</s> according to its taste; what then? It is pungent in <s>vipāka</s>, because it is produced from varied causes.

children.text: śūkaro madhurarasayukto guruguṇopetaśca yathārasaṃ madhuravipāka eva samānapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: A pig, though possessed of sweet taste and the heavy quality, has precisely sweet <s>vipāka</s> according to its taste, because it is produced from identical causes.

children.text: evaṃ yāni samānapratyayārabdhāni dravyāṇi teṣāṃ rasopadeśenaiva guṇā nirdiṣṭā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, for substances that are produced from identical causes, the qualities are indicated simply by teaching their taste.
And accordingly the sage says:
A substance that is cold in <s>vīrya</s> and sweet in taste and digestion,

children.text: tayoramlaṃ yaduṣṇaṃ ca yaccoktaṃ kaṭukaṃ tayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: and that which is sour in those two and hot, and that which is said to be pungent in those two ...
Their collection of qualities has been indicated by the teaching on taste,
and, since they are not contrary in respect of potency, it will also be taught from the standpoint of post-digestive effect.

children.text: yathā payo yathā sarpiryathā vā cavyacitrakau
children.translated_text: Just as milk, just as ghee, or just as <s>cavya</s> and <s>citraka</s>,
so also other such substances should be indicated by the physician from the standpoint of taste.
Thus.

children.text: bāhulyena ca rasādisamānapratyayārabdhānyeva dravyāṇīti cetasi kṛtvācāryo 'vocat
children.translated_text: And because substances are for the most part produced from similar causes such as taste and the rest, the teacher, keeping this in mind, said:

children.text: yathā gurvādayo guṇā dravye pṛthivyādau rasāśraye
children.translated_text: As the qualities beginning with heaviness, in a substance such as earth which is the substrate of taste,
are ascribed to the tastes by a figurative usage based on association.
Thus.

children.text: ata eva ca bahutarāṇi dravyāṇi rasādisamānapratyayārabdhāni ato rasopadeśavyāptyā tāni nirdeṣṭuṃ śakyante nānyathā ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason, since very many substances are produced from similar causes such as taste and the rest, they can be indicated through the scope of the teaching on taste, and not otherwise.

children.text: vicitrapratyayārabdhāni punaḥ katipayānyeva dravyāṇi tāni pratidravyam evopadiśyante ||
children.translated_text: But the substances produced from complex causes are only a few; they are taught substance by substance.
The sage too has stated this matter precisely by reasoning:

children.text: yathā madhuraṃ kiṃcid uṣṇaṃ syātkaṣāyaṃ tiktameva ca
children.translated_text: For example, something sweet may be hot, and something astringent may indeed be bitter,
as <s>mahatpañcamūla</s> is, and as marshland meat is.
The salt <s>saindhava</s> is not hot, just as <s>āmalaka</s> is sour;
and among bitter substances, <s>arka</s>, <s>aguru</s>, and <s>guḍūcī</s> are said to be hot.

children.text: kiṃcid amlarasaṃ grāhi kiṃcid amlaṃ bhinatti ca
children.translated_text: Some sour-tasting substance is constipating, while some sour substance breaks up the stool;

children.text: yathā kapitthaṃ saṃgrāhi bhedi cāmalakaṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: for example, <s>kapittha</s> is constipating, while <s>āmalaka</s> is purgative.
<s>Pippalī</s> and <s>nāgara</s> are aphrodisiac though pungent, while pungent is also said to be non-aphrodisiac.
Astringent is restraining and cold; in the case of <s>abhayā</s>, it is considered otherwise.
Therefore one should not prescribe every substance merely by the teaching on taste.
Thus.

children.text: ye ca rasasaṃyogā vakṣyamāṇāste rasādisamānapratyayārabdhair madhurāmlalavaṇatiktakaṭukaṣāyarūpair mithaḥ kalpanīyāḥ na tu vicitrapratyayārabdhair madhurāmlalavaṇatiktakaṭukaṣāyarūpaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the taste-combinations that are to be stated should be conceived as mutually formed from sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent forms that are produced from similar causes such as taste and the rest, but not from sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent forms produced from complex causes.

children.text: yasmātteṣāṃ na yathāśāstranirūpitā rasavīryavipākādayo vidyante vicitrapratyayārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: For their taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and so on are not present as determined according to the treatise, because they are produced from complex causes.

children.text: ato rasopadeśavyāptyā tair dravyaiste rasasaṃyogāḥ kalpayituṃ na yujyante ||
children.translated_text: Therefore it is not proper to construct those taste-combinations with such substances through the scope of the teaching on taste.

children.text: ayaṃ rasasaṃyogabheda evaṃ guṇo'yamevaṃguṇaḥ evaṃguṇatvāc cāmuṣmin viṣaye yojya etasmin viṣaye cāyamiti nirdeṣṭuṃ na śakyate anirjñātasvarūpatvāt ||
children.translated_text: It is not possible to specify: 'This very variety of taste-combination has this quality; it has such-and-such a quality, and because it has such qualities it should be applied in that case, while this one should be applied in this case,' because its own nature is not ascertained.

children.text: na hi vicitrapratyayārabdhairye rasasaṃyogāḥ kriyante teṣāṃ svarūpaṃ katham apyavadhārayituṃ śakyate ||
children.translated_text: For taste-combinations made with substances produced from complex causes cannot in any way have their nature determined.

children.text: api ca samānapratyayārabdhair ye saṃyogāḥ kalpyante teṣāṃ saṃyogināṃ vīryato yo virodhaḥ śītoṣṇalakṣaṇaḥ sa na doṣāya ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, in the combinations conceived with substances produced from similar causes, the opposition among the combined substances in respect of potency, characterized as cold and hot, is not a fault.

children.text: ye tu vicitrapratyayārabdhaiḥ saṃyogāḥ kalpyante teṣāṃ saṃyogināṃ yaḥ śītoṣṇalakṣaṇo virodhaḥ sa doṣāyeti vedyam ||
children.translated_text: But in combinations conceived with substances produced from complex causes, the opposition among the combined substances characterized as cold and hot should be understood as a fault.

children.text: anyathā rasālāpānakādīnām anekadravyakṛtānām anabhyavahāra eva prāpnuyāt ||
children.translated_text: Otherwise it would follow that drinks such as <s>rasālā</s> and <s>pānaka</s>, made from many substances, could not be consumed at all.

children.text: tathā trayastriṃśadvargā ye vakṣyamāṇāsteṣu yadayaugikaṃ taj jahyāt yaugikaṃ tv anuktamapi yuñjyād iti yadvakṣyate tatra rasādisamānapratyayārabdham eva yojyam na vicitrapratyayārabdham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, regarding the thirty-three groups that will be stated, when it will be said there that what is unsuitable should be rejected and what is suitable should be employed even if not stated, only what is produced from similar causes such as taste and the rest is to be applied, not what is produced from complex causes.
For it is impossible to determine its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect.
Therefore, and so on.

children.text: yata evaṃ vicitrapratyayārabdhaṃ vicitrarūpam tasmādrasopadeśena na tatsarvaṃ dravyamādiśet api tu rasādisamānapratyayārabdham eva dravyaṃ rasopadeśena nirdiśed iti ||
children.translated_text: Since, in this way, what is produced from complex causes has a complex form, therefore one should not prescribe all such substances merely by the teaching on taste; rather, one should indicate by the teaching on taste only a substance produced from similar causes such as taste and the rest.

children.text: iti śrīmṛgāṅkadattaputraśrīmadaruṇadattaviracitāyām aṣṭāṅgahṛdayaṭīkāyāṃ sarvāṅgasundarākhyāyāṃ sūtrasthāne dravyādivijñānīyādhyāyo navamaḥ samāptaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the ninth chapter, named 'Knowledge of substances and the rest,' in the section on principles, in the commentary on the <s>Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya</s> called <s>Sarvāṅgasundarā</s>, composed by the venerable <s>Aruṇadatta</s>, son of the venerable <s>Mṛgāṅkadatta</s>.
<s>Madana</s> is <s>rāṭha</s>.
<s>Madhuka</s> is <s>madhuyaṣṭikā</s>.
<s>Lambā</s> is known by the names <s>tumbī</s> and <s>dīrghatiktālābu</s>.
<s>Nimba</s> is <s>picumanda</s>.
<s>Bimbī</s> is <s>gohlā</s>, known by the name 'fruit resembling lips.'
<s>Viśālā</s> is <s>indravāruṇī</s>.
<s>Trapusa</s> should be understood as bitter <s>trapusa</s>, because it is suitable for emesis.
<s>Kuṭaja</s> is <s>vatsaka</s>.
<s>Mūrvā</s> is <s>pīluparṇī</s>.
<s>Devadālī</s> is <s>garāgarī</s>.
<s>Kṛmighna</s> is <s>viḍaṅga</s>.
<s>Vidula</s> is water-rattan.
<s>Dahana</s> is <s>citraka</s>.
<s>Citrā</s> is <s>mūṣikaparṇī</s>.

children.text: kośavatyau ghaṇṭālike ekā dhāmārgavo dvitīyā rājakośātakī ||
children.translated_text: The two <s>kośavatī</s> plants are the two <s>ghaṇṭālikā</s> plants: one is <s>dhāmārgava</s>, the second is <s>rājakośātakī</s>.
<s>Karañja</s> is <s>naktamāla</s>.
<s>Kaṇā</s> is <s>kṛṣṇā</s>.
The salt is <s>saindhava</s>.
<s>Vacā</s> is <s>golomī</s>.
<s>Elā</s> is <s>truṭi</s>.
<s>Sarṣapa</s> is <s>rakṣoghna</s>.
These substances beginning with <s>madana</s> are emetics, agents that cause vomiting.
If there is a pause after eight sages, then the metre is <s>mālinī</s>: 'nau mayau yaḥ.'
And here the fruits of <s>madana</s>, <s>viśālā</s>, <s>trapusa</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, <s>elā</s>, and <s>sarṣapa</s> cause emesis.
But the roots of <s>madhuka</s>, <s>vidula</s>, <s>citraka</s>, <s>dantī</s>, and <s>vacā</s> are used.
The barks of <s>rodhra</s>, <s>suvarṇakṣīrī</s>, and <s>kampilla</s> are used.
For the remaining ones, the fruits, leaves, and flowers should be understood as the parts to be used.
<s>Nikumbha</s> is <s>dantī</s>.
<s>Kumbha</s> is <s>trivṛt</s>.
<s>Triphalā</s> is <s>varā</s>.
<s>Gavākṣī</s> is <s>viśālā</s>, the second <s>indravāruṇī</s>.
<s>Snuk</s> is <s>guḍā</s>.
<s>Śaṅkhinī</s> is <s>yavatiktā</s>.
<s>Nīlinī</s> has blue flowers and is known by the name <s>bhāravāhī</s>.
<s>Tilvaka</s> is <s>rodhra</s>.
<s>Śamyāka</s> is <s>karṇikāra</s>.
<s>Kampillaka</s> is <s>rañjanaka</s>.
<s>Hemadugdhā</s> is <s>kanakakṣīrī</s>.
<s>Dugdha</s> means milk.
<s>Mūtra</s> is well known.
These, beginning with <s>nikumbha</s>, are purgatives.
<s>Upajāti</s> is the meter.
<s>Madana</s> is the fruit of <s>madana</s>.
<s>Kuṭaja</s> is the bark of <s>vatsaka</s>.
<s>Kuṣṭha</s> is named <s>gada</s>.
<s>Dāru</s> is <s>devadāru</s>.
<s>Rāsnā</s> is <s>yuktarasā</s>.
<s>Miśi</s> is <s>śatapuṣpā</s>.
<s>Kṛtavedhana</s> is <s>dhāmārgava</s>.
<s>Kulattha</s> is well known.
These are agents for evacuative enemas, that is, means for <s>nirūhaṇa</s>.

children.text: bhavati jagati nau tataḥ parau yair najasahitair jaragaiś ca puṣpitāgrā ||
children.translated_text: The meter is <s>puṣpitāgrā</s> when, after <s>na</s> and <s>ja</s> with <s>sa</s>, there are <s>ja</s>, <s>ra</s>, and <s>ga</s>; in the world the two beyond them are <s>nau</s>.
<s>Vella</s> is <s>viḍaṅga</s>.
<s>Apāmārga</s> is <s>pratyakpuṣpī</s>.
<s>Vyoṣa</s> is the three pungents.
<s>Dārvī</s> is the yellow tree.
<s>Surālā</s> is the best resin of <s>sarja</s>.
<s>Śairīṣa</s> is the seed of <s>śirīṣa</s>.
<s>Bārhata</s> is the seed of <s>bṛhatī</s>.
<s>Śaigrava</s> is the seed of <s>śigru</s>.
<s>Sāra</s>, in the case of <s>mādhūka</s>, is the essence of the flowers of <s>madhūka</s>.
<s>Saindhava</s> is what is produced from the <s>Sindhu</s> region.
<s>Tārkṣyaśaila</s> is dried <s>rasāñjana</s>.
The two <s>truṭi</s>s are small cardamom and large cardamom.
<s>Pṛthvīkā</s> is <s>hiṅgupattrī</s>.
These cleanse the upper part of the body; the meaning is that they are agents for head-purgation.
The meter named <s>vaiśvadevī</s> has <s>ma</s>, <s>ya</s>, and five <s>aśva</s>s.
<s>Bhadradāru</s> is <s>kilima</s>.
<s>Nata</s> is <s>tagara</s>.
<s>Kuṣṭha</s> is <s>gada</s>.
<s>Daśamūla</s> is the two pentads of roots.
The two <s>balā</s>s are <s>balā</s> and <s>atibalā</s>.

children.text: etāni bhadradārvādīni cāparaṃ vakṣyamāṇo vīratarādir vidāryādiśca gaṇo vāyuṃ nāśayati ||
children.translated_text: These, beginning with <s>bhadradāru</s>, and also the further group beginning with <s>vīratarā</s> and the group beginning with <s>vidārī</s> that will be stated below, destroy <s>vāyu</s>.
<s>Dūrvā</s> is <s>śādvala</s>.
<s>Anantā</s> is <s>yavāsaka</s>.
<s>Nimba</s> is well known.
<s>Vāsā</s> is <s>āṭarūṣaka</s>.
<s>Ātmaguptā</s> is <s>kapikacchū</s>.
<s>Gundrā</s> is <s>padaeraka</s>.
<s>Abhīru</s> is <s>śatāvarī</s>.
<s>Śītapākī</s> is <s>śikhaṇḍikā</s>, a variety of <s>kākaṇantikā</s>.
<s>Priyaṅgu</s> is <s>śyāmā</s>.

children.text: eṣa dūrvādirgaṇaḥ tathā vakṣyamāṇo nyagrodhādiḥ padmakādiśca gaṇaḥ tathā śāliparṇīpṛśniparṇyau tathā padmaṃ jalajam vanyaṃ kuṭannaṭam tathā sārivādiśca gaṇa ete pittaṃ nāśayanti ||
